keyPoints.en: It describes how an algorithm's work grows with input size.
It is commonly expressed with Big O notation.
It focuses on growth, not exact elapsed time.

answer.en: Time complexity describes how the amount of work grows as the input gets larger. I often use Big O notation to discuss that growth. It does not tell me the exact number of milliseconds on a specific machine.

followUp.en: What is the time complexity of searching an unsorted list?

commonMistake.en: Do not confuse Big O growth with a guaranteed runtime in seconds.

interviewCards.source: Reason: This card asks how algorithm work grows with input size, rather than elapsed runtime.

question.en: When would you use a map instead of a list?

keyPoints.en: A map stores values under keys.
It supports direct lookup when the key is known.
Choose it when key-based access fits the data.

answer.en: I use a map when I need to find a value by a meaningful key, such as a user ID. That makes the code clearer than searching a list each time. If order or repeated values matter more, a list may be a better fit.

followUp.en: What should you consider if two records can have the same key?

commonMistake.en: Do not assume that a map is the best choice for every collection.

interviewCards.source: Reason: This card compares key-based lookup in maps with ordered or repeated values in lists.

quiz.source: Reason: This question checks the work growth of scanning an unsorted collection.

question.en: What is the worst-case time complexity of scanning an unsorted list for a value?

options.en: O(n), because each item may need to be checked
O(1), because the list has a known first item
O(log n), because each check halves the list
O(n squared), because each item checks every other item

why.en: In the worst case, a scan checks each of the n items once.

tip.en: A sorted collection can support different search strategies.

quiz.source: Reason: This question compares key-based lookup with ordered collection access.

question.en: Which collection is a natural fit for looking up a user by ID?

options.en: A map that associates each user ID with a user
A list that stores users in their original order
A queue that returns users in insertion order
A stack that returns users in reverse insertion order

why.en: A map directly associates a key such as an ID with its value.

tip.en: Choose a list when order or repeated values are important.

quiz.source: Reason: This question checks the last-in-first-out behavior of a stack.

question.en: Which item does a stack usually remove first?

options.en: The next item in insertion order
The item with the highest priority

tip.en: A queue uses first-in-first-out order instead.

quiz.source: Reason: This question checks the precondition and shrinking search range of binary search.

question.en: What property does binary search normally require?

options.en: The searchable values are ordered by the searched key
The searchable values are stored in a linked structure
The searchable values contain no duplicate entries
The searchable values are grouped by their insertion time

why.en: Binary search uses ordering to discard half of the remaining range.

tip.en: Without a suitable ordering, a linear scan may be more appropriate.

quiz.source: Reason: This question distinguishes constant-time growth from an exact measured duration.

question.en: An O(1) operation takes the same number of milliseconds on every device.

why.en: O(1) describes growth that does not depend on input size, not exact elapsed time.

tip.en: Actual runtime can still vary with hardware, load, and implementation.
